summary: Aggressive, toothy ambush predator found in slow rivers, lakes and bays across southern New Brunswick and southwestern/central Nova Scotia. Introduced to both provinces and now classified as invasive — as of 2026, anglers in specific NB Recreational Fishery Areas and across all of Nova Scotia are legally required to kill and keep any chain pickerel they catch, not release it.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md:
Chain pickerel (*Esox niger*) are slender, torpedo-shaped members of the pike family, identified by a chain-like dark green mesh pattern over a lighter green-gold body and a distinct dark vertical (sometimes diagonal) bar running down from the eye. They have a duck-bill-shaped snout packed with sharp teeth. Most fish caught in this region run 12–20 inches; anything over 24 inches is a very good fish for the Maritimes.

They're classic "lie and wait" ambush predators — they hold tight to weed edges, lily pads, and submerged wood, then explosively strike baitfish, frogs, and even small ducklings that pass by. Chain pickerel are not native to the Maritimes: they were illegally introduced to southwestern Nova Scotia in the 1940s and later turned up in southern New Brunswick, and have since spread through additional watersheds via both natural movement and further illegal bucket-dumping. Wherever they establish, they're documented to hammer native brook trout populations hard, sometimes within just a few years.

sources.label: Nova Scotia Invasive Species Council, Chain Pickerel
USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species, Chain Pickerel factsheet

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
**New Brunswick:** established in the lower Saint John River system and its warm, weedy bays — Belleisle Bay, Washademoak Lake, Grand Lake, and connected waters like the Kennebecasis and Hammond rivers are all reported pickerel water by local anglers. Miramichi Lake is another spot where they show up May through September.

**Nova Scotia:** concentrated in southwestern NS (Yarmouth/Shelburne/Queens counties) where they were first released, having since spread into additional watersheds province-wide.

Look for slow current, lily pads, cattails, and drop-offs along weed edges — these fish rarely stray far from cover.

sources.label: New Brunswick Fishing Forum, Favourite Pickerel Spots
Nova Scotia Invasive Species Council, Chain Pickerel

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md:
### Season
Chain pickerel spawn very early in spring, right after ice-out, often before most other species get moving. This is prime time — pre-spawn and post-spawn fish feed heavily and are at peak weight, and they'll push into shallow coves and channels they wouldn't normally use once water temperatures climb into the mid-to-high 40s°F.

### Through the Season
Once vegetation fills in for summer, pickerel tuck into weed edges and pads and hold there into fall. They also bite well through the ice — pickerel are a common winter target in Maritime lakes.

sources.label: The Current Angler, Early Season Tactics for Chain Pickerel

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Rod | 6.5–7 ft medium-light spinning rod — same outfit you'd use for bass or trout. |
| Line | 8–12 lb monofilament or braid with a fluorocarbon leader. |
| Leader | Add a short wire or heavy fluorocarbon leader — pickerel have a mouthful of sharp teeth that will slice straight through light line. |
| Lures | Spinnerbaits, spoons, small jerkbaits, and topwater baits in white, red/white, or yellow, plus natural baitfish patterns. |
| Extras | Long-nose pliers or a jaw spreader for hook removal — do not put fingers near the teeth. |

sources.label: FishingBooker, How to Go Chain Pickerel Fishing

sections.heading: Technique
sections.body_md:
1. Target weed edges, lily pad clusters, and submerged wood rather than open water — pickerel almost never chase far from cover.
2. Work lures with a slow, erratic retrieve punctuated by pauses — an injured, struggling baitfish pattern draws the most strikes.
3. In early spring, fan-cast shallow coves and channel edges where warming water pulls baitfish (and pickerel) in first.
4. In summer, cast parallel to weed lines and pad edges rather than straight into them, working the lure along the entire edge.
5. Set the hook firmly and quickly — pickerel have hard, bony mouths, and a soft hookset often results in a missed fish.

sources.label: MeatEater Fishing, Lake Snake Love: How to Catch Chain Pickerel

sections.heading: Handling & Release — Read This Before You Let One Go
sections.body_md:
This is the single most important thing to know about chain pickerel in this region: **in many NB and all NS waters, you are now legally required to keep every chain pickerel you catch, not release it.**

Effective April 1, 2026, New Brunswick added a mandatory condition of licence requiring anglers to retain (not release) chain pickerel caught in these Recreational Fishery Areas (RFAs): **Restigouche, Chaleur, Miramichi, Southeast, and Inner Bay of Fundy.** Releasing one back can draw a fine of $100–$500 under the Fish and Wildlife Act. Fish must be humanely euthanized immediately (a swift, firm blow to the head is the standard method) and can be kept for consumption or delivered frozen to a local Department of Natural Resources office; catches should also be reported to DNR with date, location, and photos where possible.

Nova Scotia's approach goes further: anyone fishing under a sportfishing licence agrees, as a condition of that licence, to retain any chain pickerel caught anywhere in the province — there is no release option once you've hooked one.

**Before you fish anywhere for chain pickerel in NB, confirm which RFA you're in** using GNB's Fishing Regulations Web/Mobile Map, since the mandatory-retention rule is defined by specific RFAs, not a blanket province-wide rule the way it is in NS.

sources.label: Government of New Brunswick, New recreational fishing rules to take effect
Government of New Brunswick, Mandatory retention of invasive species
Government of New Brunswick, Fish NB Angling Regulations (regulations summary)

sections.heading: Conservation & Consumption Notes
sections.body_md:
Chain pickerel are not a conservation concern themselves — quite the opposite. Fisheries managers in both provinces treat them as a damaging invasive species that outcompetes native fish (including brook trout and Atlantic salmon fry) for food and habitat, which is the whole reason behind the retention requirement. Do not use chain pickerel as live or dead bait, and never transport live pickerel between waterbodies — that's exactly how the species has continued to spread. Clean boats, waders, and bait buckets between trips to different lakes.

As table fare, pickerel are bony (Y-bones like their pike relatives) but the flesh is white, mild, and good eating once you learn to fillet around the bones.

sources.label: Nova Scotia Invasive Species Council, Chain Pickerel
Mi'kmaq-Maliseet Nations News, Chain Pickerel, An Aquatic Invasive Species

variants.name: Northern Pike
variants.how_to_tell: Chain pickerel show a dark, chain-like mesh pattern over a lighter green-gold body, with both the cheek and the entire gill cover (operculum) fully covered in scales. Northern pike are larger-growing, with light, bean-shaped cream or yellow spots scattered across a darker olive-green to brown body — the opposite light-on-dark pattern from a pickerel's dark-on-light mesh — and only the cheek is fully scaled; the lower half of the gill cover is bare of scales.
variants.where_found: Reported as an increasingly encountered fish in the Saint John River drainage (NB) as pike move in from neighbouring Maine waters; not yet a long-established Maritime population the way chain pickerel is.
variants.notes: Getting this wrong matters in the wrong direction here too: chain pickerel is a mandatory-keep invasive in several NB RFAs and province-wide in NS, while northern pike is not currently subject to the same mandatory-retention rule in this region — confirm the species carefully before deciding whether a fish must be kept.

variants.name: Muskellunge
variants.how_to_tell: Chain pickerel have both cheek and gill cover fully scaled and typically fewer than 120 lateral line scales in the low range for the genus. Muskellunge are the largest esocid, with only the upper portion of the cheek and gill cover scaled (the rest bare), dark spots or vertical bars on a lighter body (opposite of a pickerel's dark mesh-on-light-body look), and six or more sensory pores per side on the underside of the lower jaw versus a pickerel's fewer pores.
variants.where_found: Saint John River, New Brunswick, particularly near the Meduxnekeag River — an introduced, unwanted population that established itself in the mid-2000s.
variants.notes: Muskellunge is not currently a mandatory-retention species in NB the way chain pickerel is in several RFAs — do not assume the same keep-it-rule applies just because both are toothy esocids caught in the same water.
